did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ezra’s report concerned not only the people, but also the priests and Levites: according to the officials, they too had not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands.
Did you know? The officials pointed out that the leaders and officials were the first to act unfaithfully, meaning the offense was not limited to ordinary people.
Did you know? Ezra’s first response when he heard these things was an intense act of mourning: he tore his garments and robe, pulled out the hair from his head and beard, and sat in shock.

Did you know? Everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel gathered around Ezra. They remained with him until the evening offering, expressing their shared grief and collective soul-searching.
Did you know? Ezra prayed after his fast, at the time of the evening offering: he fell on his knees and spread out his hands toward the LORD.
Did you know? In his prayer, Ezra does not blame only others but speaks in the plural: “our sins” and “our guilt,” acknowledging the people’s shared responsibility.

Did you know? In the midst of his confession, Ezra also recalls the LORD’s kindness: the LORD left the people a remnant, gave them “a peg” in His holy place, enlightened their eyes, and granted them a little relief.
Did you know? Ezra describes the people’s condition as slavery, yet emphasizes that even in this state the LORD did not abandon them but extended kindness to them before the kings of Persia.
Did you know? After recalling the kindness shown to the people, Ezra asks in anguish, “What can we say after this?”—How could they forsake the LORD’s commandments after all this goodness?
Did you know? Ezra’s prayer ends with a twofold acknowledgment: the LORD is righteous, while the people stand before Him in their guilt, with no grounds to claim innocence for their actions.
